summary: Describes what the IETF actually is: an organization defined by its participants and processes, not by a formal membership or legal entity. Earlier documents used the term without defining it. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: People kept saying 'the IETF' without ever explaining what it is. RFC 3233 explains that it is a large open community of engineers who write Internet specifications, not a company with a board or formal members. It is a Best Current Practice, and it points to other documents that describe how the group works.

subtitle: A short note that says what 'the IETF' means: an open community, not a company or a club with formal membership.

tldr.problem: Many RFCs say 'the IETF' as if it were an already-defined entity, but no IETF document had correctly defined it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the IETF as an open global community of network designers, operators, vendors and researchers, and points to BCP 9, BCP 10 and BCP 11 for its structure and procedures.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 58) that gives one reference definition: the IETF is an unincorporated, freestanding organization partly supported by the Internet Society.

today: RFC 3233 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 58), and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Definition Was Needed
sections.content: Many RFCs refer to the IETF, and many important IETF documents speak of it as if it were already a defined entity. As the abstract puts it, no IETF document correctly defines what the IETF is. This document supplies a more concrete definition as it was understood at the time of writing. Even BCP 9 (RFC 2026), the primary document describing the Internet standards process, never defines the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: People used a name for years without writing down exactly what it meant. This short note writes it down.

sections.title: What the IETF Is
sections.content:
As described in BCP 11 (RFC 2028), the Internet Engineering Task Force is an open global community of network designers, operators, vendors and researchers producing technical specifications for the evolution of the Internet architecture and the smooth operation of the Internet.

The RFC stresses that the IETF is not a corporation: it is an unincorporated, freestanding organization. It has no board of directors, no formally signed bylaws and no treasurer. Its structure, including its leadership, its working groups and the definition of IETF membership, is described in BCP 11, and the procedures for choosing its leadership are in BCP 10 (RFC 2727). So when RFCs say 'the IETF', they mean the group that acts in accordance with BCP 9, BCP 10 and BCP 11.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF is a loose, worldwide group of people who build and run networks. It has no office of a president and no official bank of its own. Other documents describe how the group is organized and how it chooses its leaders.

sections.title: The IETF and the Internet Society
sections.content:
The IETF is partially supported by the Internet Society (ISOC), an international non-profit organization incorporated in the US with thousands of individual and corporate members throughout the world who pay membership fees. ISOC provides many services to the IETF, including insurance and some financial and logistical support.

Internet standardization is an organized activity of ISOC, and the ISOC Board of Trustees is responsible for ratifying the procedures and rules of the Internet standards process. The IETF is not a formal subset of ISOC, however: for example, one does not have to join ISOC to be a member of the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: A separate non-profit society pays for insurance and gives some money and staff help. But you can take part in the IETF without joining that society.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that all IETF protocols must describe the security aspects of the environment in which they will be used, and that the IETF has a Security Area that discusses the security aspects of IETF protocols. Descriptive documents such as this one, it says, do not affect the security of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: This note only describes a group of people, so it does not change how safe the Internet is.
